A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-leakage study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renumbering, relocation and the expanded experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original student-model training and judgment experiments, preference leakage scores, recognition experiments and human annotation results, including Appendix B.3.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds feature-removal, mitigation, prompt-sensitivity, statistical, Chinese-language and expanded model-comparison results.

M1.justification: v3 supplements the retained generator–student–judge framework with evaluation-time paraphrasing and bias corrections estimated from held-out data, including context-dependent corrections at inference (Section 5.8, Appendix C.4). These are supplementary judging procedures; the original student-training workflow and PLS calculation remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds Chinese synthetic SFT data using Moss-3 instructions and evaluation on m-ArenaHard and XAlpacaEval (Appendix D.5). It also evaluates mitigation on a human-labeled corpus assembled from PPE, MTBench and Human Preference (Section 5.8, Appendix C.4). This expands language and judgment-task coverage beyond v2; the Chatbot Arena-to-LMArena rename itself adds no coverage.

E2.justification: The original judge and SFT/DPO/ICL comparisons are retained. v3 adds a comparison of the unmodified judge with prompting, chain-of-thought, paraphrasing, auto-calibration and contextual calibration (Table 7), plus three Claude-3.5-Sonnet judge pairs for both student models (Table 13).

E3.justification: New protocols include rewritten evaluation prompts, additional LLaMA and smaller Qwen student configurations, feature removal using Qwen-3-8B, and human-label-based Error Bias evaluation with held-out calibration sets. Gemini-2.0 is used specifically for the new feature-removal experiment (Section 5.7); the original main experiment's models and 30,000-prompt training setup are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds interventions removing style, formatting or wording to test their contribution to leakage (Table 6), a mitigation comparison (Table 7), and rewritten-prompt sensitivity analysis (Table 10). It also extends student-size sensitivity and tests Chinese-language generalization. The existing mixing, relatedness, learning-method, recognition and category analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 reports point estimates and annotator agreement without repeated-run variability or significance tests. v3 first reports three repeated experiments with means and variances (Appendix D.2, Table 9), and a nonparametric bootstrap with 10,000 resamples over 500 ArenaHard prompts to test PLS > 0 (Appendix D.4, Table 11). This does not establish an increase from a previously specified run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their values, while substantial new results appear. In the new feature-removal setting, GPT–Gemini PLS is 17.5% at baseline and 9.0% without style (Table 6). Error Bias is 17.8 at baseline and 7.3 with contextual calibration (Table 7). Tables 9–14 add statistical, prompt, Chinese-language, Claude-pair and expanded scaling results; these are additional comparisons, not improvements over v2's original scores.

T1.justification: The formal preference-leakage definition, relatedness formulations, PLS formula and worked calculation remain unchanged. v3 introduces Error Bias as the difference between two normalized directional judgment-error rates (Section 5.8 and Appendix D.8, Equation 10). No new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, three research questions, contribution list and concluding scientific claims retain the same central message: generator–judge relatedness produces widespread, subtle preference leakage. The additional experiments support and investigate these claims without redefining the central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 develops the earlier suggestion about inherited stylistic features into a detailed interpretation of style and formatting as leakage mechanisms, including claims about differences between judge families (Section 5.7). It adds calibration implications and an external-detector proposal, and qualifies the leaderboard case study through missing distillation metadata and prohibitive re-evaluation costs (Sections 5.4–5.5).

D1.justification: v3 identifies the rewriting model, explains the Gemini-2.0 substitution, and describes mitigation-corpus filtering, log-probability-based calibration and context-dependent held-out adjustments. Original training hyperparameters, hardware, prompts and repository disclosure are retained. The added reproducibility statement promises further materials, but precise calibration sample counts, prompts and seed values are not supplied.

R1.justification: v3 adds background citations, including Qu et al. (2025) and newer Li et al. works, together with sources for the mitigation datasets. The related-work discussion and positioning against egocentric bias and traditional data leakage remain substantively unchanged; much of the reference editing is conversion to author–year style.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v3 makes localized explanatory revisions, adds Sections 5.7–5.8 and an organized additional-experiments appendix, and introduces ethics, reproducibility, acknowledgment and writing-assistance statements. This is an expansion with limited rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The original win-rate plots move from v2's main text to v3's Appendix D.1 as Figures 5–6. The scaling bar chart becomes a scatterplot of average PLS against model size with family trend lines and additional models (v3 Figure 2a). Eight new tables substantially expand the displays, alongside conversion to the ICLR layout; the category, human-annotation and annotation-tool figures are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 improves support for the leakage findings by adding uncertainty reporting and tests of prompt, language and judge generalization, while feature-removal and mitigation experiments provide useful additional evidence. The gains are limited by incomplete mitigation protocols and unexplained numerical differences: Mistral's LLaMA–Gemini ArenaHard PLS is 13.1% in retained Table 1 but 7.4% in new Table 11. The evidence base improves, although the new analyses require clearer documentation and reconciliation.
